evidence: Class decorators: @Injectable() and constructor @Inject(TOKEN) from @nestjs/common. These are DI wiring, not types in a signature, and the decorator ban applies only to domain files.
register(dto: RegisterAttendeeDto): Promise<RegistrationResponseDto> uses project-declared DTOs under src/registrations/dto (application layer).
Constructor fields are typed with domain-declared ports: WorkshopRepository, AttendeeRepository and RegistrationRepository.
throw new DomainError('not-found', ...) uses the project's domain error, not an HTTP exception.
Business decisions are delegated: this.policy.assertCanRegister(...), workshop.takeSeat(), registration.cancel(new Date()).
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
src/registrations/registrations.service.ts fits the application-layer role. RegistrationsService coordinates use cases: it loads aggregates through repository ports declared in the domain, hands the eligibility decision to the domain RegistrationPolicy and the entity methods (takeSeat, releaseSeat, cancel), saves the results, and maps them to application DTOs.

The NestJS @Injectable and @Inject decorators are dependency-injection wiring. The rubric bans framework decorators only in domain files. For application files it bans framework types in signatures, and no NestJS type appears in any parameter, return or field type.

The parameter and return types are all project-declared: RegisterAttendeeDto and RegistrationResponseDto are application DTOs, and the repository interfaces come from the domain. Errors are raised as the project's own DomainError, not HTTP exceptions, and the file uses no status codes or request/response objects. It does no direct persistence or I/O; it only calls repository ports.
